papers.title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
papers.authors: Chang Yang, Yao Xuan, Wendan Yan, Nhat Le, Jiang Liu, Longhao Jin, Zhen Peggy Yao, Alireza Vahdatpour, Djordje Gligorijevic
papers.abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.
papers.summary: Large web platforms run fleets of ads ranking models, and inheriting old features with manual edits struggles to balance per-model serving costs against shared feature pipeline budgets. Meta built a fleet-scale system where LLM agents propose hypotheses and deterministic tools run and verify experiments, finding that ==gains usually come from rebalancing volume across feature categories, since scaling every category up hits diminishing returns==. A shared retrieval LLM, continually fine-tuned on outcomes across the fleet, shortlists cross features before deterministic importance estimators and multi-task Pareto fronts blend the rankings, and a search agent then runs asynchronous trials under serving resource caps. Before training, a trimming step swaps over-budget additions for already-used features of the same category under the same budget. Across production models, it improves NE by 0.31% on average within each model’s budget, trimming cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% on average with no regression beyond measurement noise, and launched models lift a primary online metric by 0.20% in A/B tests.

papers.title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
papers.authors: Anish Khazane, Alex Saad-Falcon, Guanchu Wu, Marcio Porto, Jasper Shan, Fei Yu, Eugene Shulga, Intaik Park, Yongzhe Zhang, Xiaoyu Deng, Sheng Luo, Xiaoya Wang
papers.abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.
papers.summary: When training large-scale recommendation models, GPU count is often constrained not by compute, but by sparse embedding tables filling up HBM. Existing in-training embedding pruning (ITEP) dynamically drops less important rows during training, yet usually sets pruning ratios by table size, ignoring feature contributions and sometimes hurting accuracy. Meta's FI-ITEP instead precomputes feature importance, such as by shuffling a feature's values within a batch and measuring the loss change, then assigns higher pruning ratios to less important tables. Across three industry-scale recommendation models, it cuts total memory by 20% to 40% while matching or beating size-based pruning in accuracy, and the same trend holds on the open-source DLRM benchmark. The freed memory lets a frequently retrained model drop from 112 to 80 GPUs with higher per-GPU throughput. ==Larger models carry more low-contribution embeddings, so the compute saved outweighs the upfront estimation cost==; for smaller models with less redundancy, size-based pruning may suffice.

papers.title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhixiong Hu, Meng Li, Maggie Zhang, Deborshi Goswami, David Bailey, James Bradley
papers.abstract: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for http://autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.
papers.summary: Autodesk recommends product pages, industry pages, customer stories, and learning content on one site, where standard item-ID sequence encoders drop web events without catalog IDs and running an LLM synchronously breaks latency budgets. LSER keeps the existing two-tower model and sequence encoder, using a fine-tuned LLM to turn raw event text into auxiliary session and history embeddings inside the user tower. Heavy encoding runs asynchronously in a nearline pipeline into an embedding store, so live requests read the stored vectors for ANN search. In offline ablation, adding these LLM features raises popular-product HR@10 by 9.6 percentage points and customer-story HR@1 by 6.0 percentage points, while other surfaces stay essentially flat. The completed online A/B test compared the nearline two-tower stack without the LLM features against the legacy rule engine, lifting product order submission rate by 14.8%, with live testing of the LLM features planned next. ==For sparse multi-content sites, refreshing raw-event LLM features nearline adds semantic signal within retrieval latency limits.==

scenario: Today's selected papers sit in large-scale production recommendation and ranking systems, focusing on how features, embeddings, and retrieval work under real scale and cost constraints. For fleet-scale ranking models, one work frames feature optimization as a cost-aware agentic system. For large-scale recommendation models, another focuses on intelligent embedding pruning. In production content recommendation, a third explores integrating LLM-based embeddings from sessions all the way into retrieval serving. Taken together, these papers span key parts of large-scale recommendation and ranking systems, from feature optimization and embedding pruning to retrieval serving.
